p: Yeah. Thank you. You know, I’m going to say a few words and then invite Dr. Braunstein back up. You know, we think that the sexual health clinics are a critical part of our infrastructure when it comes to protecting New Yorkers and providing this low to no-cost alternative for New Yorkers, and we also understand that for many New Yorkers, it’s better for them to come into one of our clinics than to go to see their doctor. There’s a level of– it’s just a better environment for them to do so. And so for those New Yorkers, we really want to make sure that we’re providing this resource. Let me hand it over to Dr. Braunstein to share a little bit more.

Thank you, Commissioner and Chair. We are really proud of our sexual health clinics. We are really a leader in the types of services, the breadth of services and the culturally responsiveness of the services that we offer in these clinics, and we know they reach the communities that need them most. So, the six sexual health clinics that are operating now, you know, offer a huge range of services, right? We are

offering sexual health services, HIV testing, STI testing including also linkage or provision of post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV, pre-exposure prophylaxis for HIV, reproductive health services including medication abortion, vaccination services for STIs. And then increasingly, as we developed more and more partnerships with community organizations in the areas that our clinics are located in, referrals for additional services that community members might need.
So, how are you maintaining or expanding access to sexual health services and prevention resources in the areas where the clinics were closed?

We do have– in addition to the sexual health clinics, we do have our funded community partners, both clinical and non-clinical who are located throughout the boroughs, and again, in high needs areas, including some of the ones that where our clinic closures have occurred. So, between the sexual health clinics, our programming, our condom distribution that happens, again, in high-priority areas, we are confident that

we are covering the needs of communities with our sexual health services.

Okay. DOHMH administers several– I’m done with HIV. You can– DOHMH administers several maternal health programs aimed at approving pregnancy outcomes and reducing infant mortality including Maternity Infant Reproduction, newborn home visiting, Nurse Family Partnership, and Universal Home Visiting programs. The Fiscal 2027 Preliminary Plan includes $49.9 million for these programs. At the same time, pregnancy-associated mortality continues to show significant racial disparities, particularly among Black women and birthing people. In the Preliminary Plan, the Maternal Infant Reproduction program was allocated $7.3 million, a nine percent reduction from $8.1 million in the Fiscal 2026 adopted plan. What specific services will be reduced as a result of this cut?

Thank you for that question, Chair. You know this is an incredibly important issue that we must remain focused on addressing and trying to close the racial and ethnic

gap. What we know from our data is that for Black birthing people, 75 percent of maternal deaths are preventable, and many of those happen in the post-discharge period which makes the work of community based and clinical support after birth very, very, very critical. We also know that Black women are four times more likely to die from pregnancy-associated death and six times more likely to die from pregnancy-related deaths versus their white counterparts. And so we have a number of different initiatives to try and meaningfully address this. One of the programs that I’m most proud of and take pride in is the Citywide Doula initiative which we will talk more about, but also, you know, interventions like the Stress Free Zone in Brownsville, and the nation’s largest Nurse Family Partnership program which does home visiting services to new parents. And so this is an issue that we remain committed to addressing. We have a number of tools in our tool kit, and we will not let up until we make an impact on this issue.
You going to address the cut?

Yeah, and just to add to that, Chair Schulman, so there has been no cut or reduction in the maternal health world. I think what you may be referring to is that the City Council funds are not baselined, so the amount that you’re seeing perhaps in the current year is a little bit higher than the funding that’s going to be in FY 27.
Okay, so what portion of the $49.9 million in maternal and child health funding is dedicated specifically to addressing racial disparities in pregnancy-associated mortality?
Thank you for that question. I’m going to hand it over to Aaron to share more on that.

So, I mean, I would say that all of our maternal work is driven by that goal. You know, one of the Healthy NYC goals, we aim to reduce the rate of pregnancy-associated death among Black, non-Hispanic women by 10 percent by 2030. It’s a central goal for

the agency. There’s no specific dedicated funding stream because the agency–
[interposing] Okay.
is oriented as a whole to addressing racial disparities in our work, and that is public health.
What metrics are being used to evaluate the impact? Of the $49.9 million to address racial disparities?

Yeah, thank you for that question. So, the metrics that we’re using are pregnancy-associated events, adverse events, pre-term labor, emergency C-sections, and of course, mortality after birth. We have other important metrics that we could share more, but those are some of the most important indicators that we look at.
How did DOHMH and H+H collaborate in improving maternal health efforts, and how do the services differ between the two?

Yeah, thank you. We work very closely with our partners at H+H to make sure that we are offering a synergistic approach and making sure that we do the best we can to provide

comprehensive maternal mental health– maternal health services. We are developing the Maternal Home Collaborative which is a delivery and payment model which helps to reduce mortality by supporting birthing people in both clinical and in community settings. And we’re exploring and moving forward with the 1115 Medicaid waiver to fund that work. We also have a number of other programs including the Home Visiting programs which provide this sort of community to clinical continuum, and H+H really is able to intervene in the health care setting in the hospital and health center setting. And so it’s really this sort of combined approach there in the traditional kind of brick and mortar, and we are in the community doing the work, but both of our teams have a role to play in making sure that we address this issue.
Are current funding levels sufficient to meet the city’s maternal health goals?
Thank you for that question. I’m going to hand it to Aaron to talk a little bit about the budget there.

One thing I would say is actually the number that you said earlier, the $49 million, is actually one piece, it’s the largest piece. But actually, when you think about the maternal health work that happens across the agency which happens in at least three different divisions–
[interposing] Okay.

It’s actually $69 million. So, it’s a substantially higher amount. I mean, we’re always thinking about resource levels and what we need to achieve goals, but I think we’re continuing those conversations.

Okay. I mean, we haven't been able, at least since I’ve been in the council, to break this pattern, so I’m hoping that you with all of your different expertise and background can help to break through here, because it’s difficult, and I worked–
[interposing] Yeah.

I worked at Woodhall where they had a large number of maternal deaths. So, it’s an issue. So whatever we can do to

be helpful, and I don’t know the, you know– I don’t have the resolution, but–
[interposing] Yeah. Well, we’re committed to making and impact on this issue and we’re committed to working with you.

And you know, some of it is the training of the docs, some of it is– you know, it’s all different ways that we– and the way that we interact with patient– the way docs interact with patients, and you know, there’s all different kinds of things. But hopefully, you’ll be able to break through that. I have confidence in you.
Thanks, Chair Schulman.

Following changes to– one second. Shaun, do you want to ask, because I have a number of questions? Do you want to? Alright. So, I’m going to break for a second. I’m going to ask Majority Leader Abreu to ask his questions, and then we’ll come back.
Great.

Thank you, Chair, and congratulations, Commissioner, to your

appointment, and I’m confident you’re going to do a great job for New York City. I have a set of questions on the sleep apnea pilot program that we passed last year. In April 2025, the Council passed Local Law 52 requiring DOHMH to establish a sleep apnea pilot program and public education outreach campaign. The Local Law established a three-year pilot program to provide access to sleep apnea screenings at no-cost, as well as access to home sleep apnea tests. This law required DOHMH to conduct a public education and outreach campaign on sleep apnea. For me, this is a very important personal bill. I suffer from sleep apnea. I know a lot of New Yorkers who suffer from it. DOHMH communicated to the Council that the pilot program started on October 13th of last year. However, we have been told as of– as recently as December 12 that the public education and outreach component was still “in development.” This morning, I visited the Sleep Disorder Lab page on DOHMH’s website which provides information on sleep apnea. However, there was no mention of the free sleep apnea screening pilot

program. How are New Yorkers supposed to access a free program that has received zero public outreach?

Yeah. Thank you for your leadership on this issue, Majority Leader. We are working closely with H+H to get information on this program, and we hope to be able to provide specifics after we convene with them and get back to you with how things are going with the program.

How fast are– what’s the turnaround you’re thinking here, because obviously we’re already beyond the deadline when this public outreach was supposed to begin? And can you speak to the mediums of public communication that your agency is looking into?

Yeah. Thank you very much. We hope to have this posted in the next few weeks, and we’re looking at every single option that we can to get outreach out to community members. We take this issue very seriously, and I think that there’s a lot that we can do to join you and your leadership in moving this issue forward and making sure that we work with community members on this.

Thank you. And just lastly, the law requires DOHMH to conduct an outreach campaign through social media, the internet, digital kiosks, and other appropriate mediums in citywide designated languages. DOHMH is required to inform the public on health risks associated with sleep apnea, common signs and symptoms of sleep apnea, and how to access health care for sleep apnea including the screening pilot program. It would be great for, you know, all of these criteria within the law to be satisfied and not just one of these requirements. And so I hope that when you look into, you know, posting this and conducting this campaign, we’re able to do the wide array of mediums that are available to you, including getting the mayor to do a social media. You know, he’s very– he has a big following. It would be great to see some kind of work there.

Thank you very much, Majority Leader. We are committed to making sure that this information gets out to individuals who have sleep apnea, and we’re looking at all the options. We’re looking forward to working with you

on this issue to identify what the best media are for getting that out.
Thank you so much, Mr. Commissioner, and congratulations again. I’m sure you’re going to do a fantastic job. Thank you, Chair.
Thank you.

You’re welcome. And I want to echo Council Member Abreu’s questions and say if you can get back to us with a specific timeline of when this will be implemented, that would be– I was a co-sponsor of the legislation. It’s very important for– particularly for people who are affected, and there’s so much that’s been coming out since the legislation was passed about this issue, and the interventions that are available and all of that. So, just give us– just come back to us with a specific timeline that, you know, so we can know.
You got it.

Thank you. Okay, Healthy NYC– I’m going to ask, like, a few more questions. So, in– so, Healthy NYC, it’s a five-year health agenda aimed at increasing life expectancy, 83

years, which we’ve met, but there are inequities still around that. What is Healthy NYC’s current operating budget, and how are funds allocated across the seven priority areas?

Yeah. Thank you, first of all, for your leadership on this issue on Healthy NYC, and we are, you know, elated that we have reached the goal of 83.2 years– of 83 years and passing it 83.2 years. We also know that work is not done. And so we remain committed to making an impact not just on this life expectancy goal, but also to continue to push forward on our work on each of these seven key drivers. So, the dedicated budget is $1.7 million which supports staff. It also supports– for health care improvement who we have on contract really helping to move the work that we’re doing each of these key drivers, on many of these key drivers, even more deeply into the work that we do. But I will say that this is really an all of agency approach. This is not just–
[interposing] Right.

people who report to me in my office. Every single staff member in our agency is working towards in some way hitting one of these drivers, and so we’re all rowing in the same direction. Let me hand it over to Aaron to see if there’s anything else to add on this.
Yeah, not much to add. Just to say that I mean arguably our whole budget could be considered, you know, an effort to advance the goals of Healthy
Yeah, because we– I mean, I think that there are ways that– I want to see– do you believe that we can meet all the indicators by 2030, the 2030 targets?
Yeah. Thank you for that. We are continuing to drive meaningful progress on each of these seven drivers, and you know, these drivers are not going to change–
[interposing] Right.

Chair Schulman, in terms of we’re not moving the goal post. And so we are committed to continuing to try and hit each one

of those. We’ve had a considerable amount of success on a couple of these. As you know, with COVID deaths being down about 93 percent, overdose deaths down about 28 percent, but there’s so much more work to do on the other drivers, and so I’m committed to mobilizing our agency to go after–
[interposing] And I would encourage– you and I have spoke about this– of getting your champion partners behind this as well.
Yeah.
Because they have a stake in it, because it affects their entities as well. So, and then we can talk offline about some other ideas around that, too, so.
That’s great.

The PMMR reports that 832 patients were diagnosed with tuberculosis in calendar year 2024, a 23 percent increase from 679 cases in 2023. The report notes that staffing shortages and limited funding have affected the Department’s ability to carry out key tuberculosis control activities including contact investigations and case management. The city’s TB response also

relies heavily on federal funding which you had mentioned earlier which may be subject to reductions. So, what factors are driving the increase in tuberculosis cases? And my second question to that, is there any correlation with an increase in homelessness?
Yeah. Thank you for that. First of all, to say, you know, we have one of the strongest TB programs in the country, and we know that TB is preventable. It’s a treatable disease.
Right.

There are a number of factors, Chair. You know, we can start locally, you know, with the federal government’s posture towards immigration activities and the chilling effect that that’s causing here locally, individuals not going to get care, not coming into our clinics, not going to Health + Hospitals, not going to other hospitals and health centers throughout the city. We can also think about it, you know, nationally. You know, we have– we’re living in an era where the federal government is strangling people’s access to

health coverage, and so people are uninsured, under-insured at higher rates. And then we can think about it globally, as well. You know, we think about the federal government’s defunding USAID. And so– and that’s one of the defensive tools that we use to internationally and globally, you know, provide the treatment that stems tuberculosis cases. We know that 90 percent of the people who we have seen as newly diagnosed with TB are non-U.S. born.
Okay.
And so, yeah, there’s a number of different factors that we think are contributing.
What strategies are we implementing to prevent further increases in TB cases, particularly in high risk communities?
Yeah. Thank you. I’m going to go ahead and ask Dr. Braunstein to come up, but as she’s doing so, we have recently received new support with regard to staffing to be able to do the work of prevention–
[interposing] Great.
do the work of treatment. But let me hand it over to Dr. Braunstein.

Thank you, Commissioner. And we, as you’ve cited, we’ve been very concerned about recent trends in tuberculosis numbers, just incredible upticks. I will share, though, our 2025 TB report, annual TB report that’s coming out in a few days, is actually going to cite an 11 percent decrease in TB cases last year which is really incredible news. And we are very hopeful that this decline will be sustained, but absolutely, though, remain vigilant and concerned to make sure that it is– it continues beyond just 2025. Yeah, as the Commissioner cited, there are really a combination of factors that have led to what we’ve seen recently in terms of trends, and I just want to speak to the point about homelessness. That has long been a factor, of course, in the–
[interposing] But there’s been a substantial increase in homelessness.

Absolutely, absolutely. But I will just cite that as you might

be aware, since 2022 the Health Department has collaborated with various city and state agencies to really enhance TB screening and services and shelters and the HERRCs, and other temporary housing sites, and these numbers are pretty incredible in terms of the reach we’ve been able to make. So between 2022 and 2025, over 30,000 individuals received on-site TB-related services through this initiative, including things like TB testing, chest x-ray services, directly observed therapy. So really, really impactful. And I will also note that you’ll see in our upcoming report that the number of people with TB who experience homelessness fell by 56 percent in 2025 compared to 2024. So, hopeful that we’re really making a dent here due to our really–
[interposing] that’s great.
incredible TB program, but certainly something we’ll remain vigilant around.
Thank you.
And Chair, I mentioned the new staff that we got. I want to hand it over to Aaron to unpack that a little bit.

Yeah, just to add, I mean, you mentioned federal dollars always being at risk including in this area. I mean, one of the optimistic things that happened recently is last year we got new funding for 79 new staff.
Oh, wow.
And over $7 million, and so that brings our total TB budget to just over $20 million with like 250 heads. So, I mean, I think while federal funding is always, you know, a concern–
[interposing] Right.
the fact that the city’s made this historic investment really decreases our reliance on federal funding and paves the path towards stability, so.

So, now I’m going to ask my last questions. So, on December– this has to do with the Health Care Price Comparison Tool. On

December 23rd, 2025, DOHMH launched New York City’s Health Care Price Comparison Tool which allows individuals to search and compare prices for 33 common health care services across the city regardless of whether they have health insurance. The tool was developed pursuant to the Health Care Accountability and Consumer Protection Act, Local Law 78 legislation introduced by Speaker Menin and is intended to increase transparency around health care costs and help New Yorkers make more informed decisions about where to seek care. Since the launch of the Health Care Price Comparison Tool in December 2025, how many users have accessed the platform and what trends has the Department observed in how residents are using the tool?

Thank you for that question, and thank you to Speaker Menin for her leadership and advocacy on this issue. You know, we think that you can’t have a conversation about affordability without having a conversation about accountable pricing, and–
Right.

just the lack of transparency that New Yorkers are suffering when it comes to deciding where to get their health care. With regard to the price comparison tool, we are tracking usage and working to expand the number of services and making sure that we increase public awareness. We can get back to you with regard to the specifics and the metrics.
Okay.
And follow up with you on what the use has been.
No, that’s fine, and you know, we have– I see that your social media has really done an uptick since you’ve joined us. But if we can do some–
[interposing] Trying, trying.

If we can do some around that, because it’s important. How does the depart– and it goes to the mayor’s, also, agenda as well. So we have a mutual agenda there. How does the Department collect and verify the pricing data

included in the tool to ensure the information is accurate and regularly updated?
Yeah, so we have pricing that is sourced through a partner at Turquoise Health.
Okay.

And so they’re aggregating price transparency data, and we’re awaiting updated contractor reports on this including pricing data and city claims as well. And so working with our partners at Turquoise as well as OLR and Milliman [sic] for that.

Yeah. And we talked about this already. So, we want to expand– when you come back with the metrics, we want to see– we really want to expand that out, so once we have that, then we should come up with a plan of how we’re going to expand that out so that people are using it, because I don’t think a lot of people know about it. I mean, we know about it because it was passed by the Council, but–
Exactly.

Give me one second. I’m now going to hand it over to my colleague Council Member Cabán. She has some questions. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Thank you. Good to see you. Congrats. Really excited to be working together. I’m going to ask you a few questions, specifically on early intervention. Early intervention offers special needs educational services for children with developmental delays, and the Preliminary Plan includes $367 million in FY 27, and that’s a 34 percent increase from the $277 million in the adopted plan from FY 26. So, can you just start by talking us through the services that are provided for early intervention, specially the health care services provided for early intervention?

Yeah. Thank you. And I’m going to start us off and then ask Deputy Commissioner Lidiya Lednyak to share more. But this program is a marvel. It’s a program that’s incredibly effective. We, in a recent Journal of the American Medical Association study, found that for children who are receiving these services, they have higher test scores in reading and in math by third

grade. And so we have a number of different intervention points and services that we use to carry out this program, and I’m going to hand it over to Deputy Commissioner Lednyak to share more. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Yeah, and in talking about those different intervention points, I think we’re also specifically interested in sort of, you know, like, what is uniquely DOHMH’s role in that intervention as opposed– you know, as it differs to ACS,
Please raise your right hand. Do you swear to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to Council Member questions?
Yes.
You may proceed.

Okay, thank you for your question. So, early intervention services and the program is a federal entitlement program for children birth to three with developmental delays and disabilities. So, early intervention services are provided without regard to race, ethnicity, income or

immigration status. Early intervention services broadly are available to eligible children, and the most typical services delivered by early intervention are service coordination which is case management, evaluation, physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech language pathology. Those are sort of the most common services. We serve 30,000 children a year. Early intervention as a program is fully administered and coordinated by the New York City Health Department. It is a separate program from any service that is offered by the New York City Public Schools or ACS, but New York City Public Schools and ACS are important referral partners to the early intervention program. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Also, I guess, in terms of the referral relationship, what happens with kind of the cross-records? How are they sort of negotiated or– like how is the information taken together and then sort of a plan made?
I’m going to pass it over to Deputy Commissioner Lidiya Lednyak on that.

Sure. so, thank you for your question. Early intervention is a completely confidential program. So, we will only share information with a system like the New York City Public Schools when we have written parental consent. So– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] A HIPAA release?
Kind of like that. We’re bound by both HIPAA and FERPA. So, which makes us– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] Okay, got it.

unique in that way for early intervention. But when we do have consent to share information, we will share information with New York City Public Schools, particularly when a child is preparing to leave early intervention right around the time they turn three and are beginning to enter, you know, New York City Public School Services, particularly the Committees on Preschool Special Education.

COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Okay. So, you’re working with a family and a child. You do a screening and, you know, you’re in the process of doing this referral to the appropriate care workers, right, to support the child. Can you just break down sort of the steps for children that have been identified to have disabilities and also how long that process takes, and then from there, do y’all have enough staff to do that? Or like, do you need more?

Thank you for your question, and also thank you for your interest in early intervention. So, when a child is identified as having say a concern about their development– and again, early intervention is a type of system where there’s no wrong door, meaning that anybody can make a referral to EI when there’s a concern about a child’s development. So, once we– once a concern is identified, they’re referred to us at the New York City Health Department. We will take the referral and assign a case manager. Every family that is referred to early intervention gets assigned a service coordinator which makes it very unique.

COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: What’s the ratio, by the way? Like, what is the case load for a case manager?

There is no established state requirement for a ratio for a case manager, but it’s about 65 children to a case manager. We have in early intervention– and I have this number. We have over 1,200 service coordinators. They are not all employed by the New York City Health Department. They are– all early intervention services are delivered by a network of over 168 service provider agencies. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Would you be able to testify anything about sort of what best practice might be in terms of case loads? I don’t know what that is? You know, nurses will know what safe staffing is. I was a defender, and I was like holy shit, you know, my caseload of 100 is way too many. So, I just am curious of like– understanding we’re always asked to do a lot with a little. The need always outpaces sort of what we have. But can you tell me kind of what would be best practice in terms of a ratio?
I think that, you know– let us come back to you with that figure. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Thanks. Sorry I interrupted you, and [inaudible] finish, yeah.

So, I just wanted to sort of finish the process for you, right? So, once a child is identified we assign a service coordinator. Then, that service coordinator helps the child receive an evaluation to determine whether the child is eligible for services, meaning whether there is a developmental delay or a disability. If a child is eligible, and around 68 percent of children are eligible who are referred, right? We have an individualized service planning meeting where we authorize a plan of care in partnership with the evaluator, case manager and the family. So, that’s sort of the whole process, and that process ideally between– from referral to the time that we have a plan is approximately 45 days. So, we– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] You said ideally, but how long is it typically taking?
So, I have that number.

And Chair, while Deputy Commissioner Lednyak is finding that, I want to turn it over to Aaron to share a little bit more about the staffing that we have, because part of your question is are we staffed up to do this work, right? So let me hand it over.

Yeah, I mean, from a funding perspective, I would say one of the most important things that’s happened in a number of years happened in the Prelim budget, and that is that the– this administration addressed a long-standing fiscal cliff for the early intervention program. So, we now have baseline funding of $79 million this year– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] Right.

growing to $144 million five years from now for the first time in a number of years which is a huge, huge win. So, that in itself stabilizes the city’s commitment to this program.

COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: And for that increase that we’re seeing in the FY 27 budget, I mean, in terms of staff lines for example, what do you anticipate that might be possible in terms of growth?
I mean, the funding that was added here was really to– a recognition of the true cost of the program that had been sort of under budgeted. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Yeah, that happens way too often.
Right. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Okay, got it.
I’ll turn it back it over.
Sure. So, 81 percent of initial ISFP meetings are held within 45 days of referral. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Sorry, what was the percentage?

81 percent.

COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Okay, thank you. Yeah. [inaudible] Okay, alright. I’ll hand it back to the Chair.

So I have– so I’m going to ask a few more questions. Some of the questions are from a colleague and member of the committee who is not here, because she’s virtual, but because we don't have a quorum, I have to ask them on her behalf. So, this is from Council Member Narcisse. We’ve seen spikes in measles and other preventable diseases nationally. What is New York City’s current risk level, and are vaccination rates where they need to be?

Thank you for that question, Chair, and thank you, Council Member Narcisse. We think it’s incredibly important that our children’s– our city’s children have access to effective vaccines, and through the Vaccine for Children’s program, we are currently able to work with over 1,200 providers. We’re vaccinated 2.5 million children every single year. And you know, we do this work every single day to make sure that we are keeping our children safe. With regard to

measles, there is at this moment, no heightened cause for alarm. We are aware that because of the federal policy shifts around vaccinations and some of the mesaging that’s coming out from the federal government, we are aware that, you know, families are getting different, you know, pieces of information and it is causing confusion, sowing doubt, eroding public trust.
Right.

And so last week we launched a brand new campaign, a paid media campaign aimed directly at this issue with regard to childhood vaccinations. And the goal of that campaign is to really get families to talk to the most trusted messengers in their lives, and these are the pediatricians.
Right.
And so, that’s some of the work that we’re doing and as it relates to the measles work.
Good. How are we measuring whether interventions are actually lowering rates of diabetes, hypertension and heart disease?
Thank you very much. I’m going to ask Dr. Zahirah to join me. You know, this is part of our routine work that we are focused on through delivering for the Healthy NYC–
[interposing] Right.

framework. As you know, cardio metabolic risk factors is a driver that we’re continuing to address here. The number of different interventions that we are focused on. I’m going to hand it over to Dr. McNatt to share more.
Please raise your right hand. Do you swear to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to Council Member questions?
Yes.
You may proceed.

Thank you so much for the question. Appreciate the opportunity to highlight some of the work around the diabetes prevention and self-management in the city. The diabetes prevention efforts are very focused on food and physical

activity across the five boroughs, and so we do a great dela of work around food and security and food affordability. Namely, we have three citywide programs in this regard that help to work on food affordability and food security as a method of prevention in diabetes and other chronic diseases. Those include Get the Good Stuff, Groceries to Go, and Health Bucks, and we’d be happy to elaborate on them. We also focus on diabetes self-management. So, once someone is diagnosed with diabetes or another chronic disease we have numerous evidence-based programs that are aimed at supporting residents once they’re diagnosed through that journey. Those programs are anywhere from five weeks to six weeks, and some are even oen year long. And they offer robust services that help folks with behavior change. They also are support groups. So, they spend a lot of time together with other people with the same diagnoses. And also our– these workshops and classes are taught by community health workers or registered dieticians and other actors, and so it’s also an opportunity to receive a great deal of education about how to speak to your health

care provider and what types of questions might help you learn more about your disease state.
